newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese dissidents in HK fear persecution.
newsitem.headline: Chinese dissidents in HK fear persecution.

text.p: Chinese dissidents living in exile in Hong Kong fear arrest or deportation to the mainland now that Beijing has resumed sovereignty over the territory, a Chinese human rights activist said.

"My strongest feeling about the handover is that I may be arrested or sent back to China at any time now," Lu Siqing, spokesman for the Information Centre of Human Rights and the Democratic Movement in China, said in an interview.
The Public Security Bureau (police) in China had warned his parents that if he stayed in Hong Kong after the handover, he could be in trouble, he told Reuters.
Lu is one of at least four dissidents who decided to stay on after the territory reverted to Chinese rule on Tuesday following a century and a half of British colonial rule.

He came to Hong Kong in 1992, one of scores of dissidents to flee their homeland amid the repression following the June 1989 Tiananmen crackdown, when Chinese troops crushed pro-democracy protests around Beijing's central square with heavy loss of life.
Many of them later found sanctuary in third countries. But, Lu said, those who stayed behind now faced serious difficulties.
"According to the law we are illegal immigrants here. From yesterday to today the situation is totally different," he said.
Although Hong Kong has been promised a high degree of autonomy under Beijing rule, Lu said, demonstrators could be arrested and prosecuted.
Yang Kang, another dissident who decided to stay on, thinks Hong Kong people should hold to their views and fight for their rights rather than wait passively for China to grant them.
"Hong Kong people should not always assume that China will shrink from killing a goose which lays golden eggs," he said.
Yang and his family have no permanent residency rights in Hong Kong and he is sure the new government will grant none. He worries about their future if they are sent back to China.
Yang was detained in China for 15 months after the Tiananmen crackdown, and came to Hong Kong in 1995 to escape persecution of his underground democratic activities on the mainland.
The former Hong Kong government helped Chinese dissidents to find asylum overseas before Beijing reasserted sovereignty and Yang said he was one of those promised help.
He said the colonial government had cheated him, persuading him to stay in Hong Kong with a false pledge of permanent residency and destruction of his illegal immigration file.
"In the last days of colonial rule, the Hong Kong government didn't want us to be a burden to them any more," he said.
"When they found no country wanted us, they persuaded us to stay. But recently I discovered that my residency will be terminated here in May 1998, I may be sent back to China then."
Lu said he disbelieved Chinese President Jiang Zemin's view that Hong Kong and China can remain totally distinct under Beijing's "one country, two systems" policy for reunification.
China was bound to influence Hong Kong, he said. "Heaven cannot exist next to hell."
